claim: β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins are ubiquitously expressed in every cell type.
source: β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins are ubiquitously expressed in every cell type and are nearly identical at the amino acid level but play vastly different roles in vivo.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the expression pattern of these actin isoforms, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins are nearly identical at the amino acid level.
source: β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins are ubiquitously expressed in every cell type and are nearly identical at the amino acid level but play vastly different roles in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work (Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1978) showing only four conservative substitutions.

claim: β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins play vastly different roles in vivo.
source: β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins are ubiquitously expressed in every cell type and are nearly identical at the amino acid level but play vastly different roles in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing different phenotypes in knockout mice.

claim: The essential roles of β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins in embryogenesis and mesenchymal cell migration critically depend on the nucleotide sequences of their genes, rather than their amino acid sequences.
source: Their essential roles in embryogenesis and mesenchymal cell migration critically depend on the nucleotide sequences of their genes, rather than their amino acid sequences
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors (Vedula et al., 2017) showing that β-actin's nucleotide sequence underlies its essential role.

claim: When targeted to the cell periphery using β-actin 3′UTR, β-actin and γ-actin have differential effects on cell migration.
source: When targeted to the cell periphery using β-actin 3′UTR; β-actin and γ-actin have differential effects on cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 demonstrating different migration rates.

claim: The differential effects of β-actin and γ-actin on cell migration directly depend on the coding sequence.
source: These effects directly depend on the coding sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using codon-switched variants showing that the coding sequence determines the phenotype.

claim: β-actin exhibits a faster translation elongation rate than γ-actin.
source: Single-molecule measurements of actin isoform translation, combined with fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, demonstrate a pronounced difference in β- and γ-actins' translation elongation rates in cells
evidence: This is directly measured using single-molecule SINAPS experiments and FRAP, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Differences in β- and γ-actin translation elongation rates lead to changes in their dynamics at focal adhesions.
source: Single-molecule measurements of actin isoform translation, combined with fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, demonstrate a pronounced difference in β- and γ-actins' translation elongation rates in cells, leading to changes in their dynamics at focal adhesions
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data showing different persistence times of actin at focal adhesions (Figure 2).

claim: Differences in β- and γ-actin translation elongation rates lead to impairments in actin bundle formation.
source: Single-molecule measurements of actin isoform translation, combined with fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, demonstrate a pronounced difference in β- and γ-actins' translation elongation rates in cells, leading to changes in their dynamics at focal adhesions, impairments in actin bundle formation
evidence: This is demonstrated by measurements of actin bundle lengths at focal adhesions (Figure 5) and supported by computational modeling.

claim: Differences in β- and γ-actin translation elongation rates lead to reduced cell anchoring to the substrate during migration.
source: Single-molecule measurements of actin isoform translation, combined with fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, demonstrate a pronounced difference in β- and γ-actins' translation elongation rates in cells, leading to changes in their dynamics at focal adhesions, impairments in actin bundle formation, and reduced cell anchoring to the substrate during migration.
evidence: This is inferred from focal adhesion analysis showing different distributions and sizes (Figure 3) and cell spreading measurements.

claim: Coding sequence-mediated differences in actin translation play a key role in cell migration.
source: Our results demonstrate that coding sequence-mediated differences in actin translation play a key role in cell migration.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data showing that coding sequence determines translation rate, which affects focal adhesions and migration.

claim: β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins share the highest identity at the amino acid level among mammalian actins, with only four conservative substitutions within their N-termini.
source: Among the six mammalian actins, β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins are the only two that are ubiquitously expressed in every mammalian cell type and share the highest identity at the amino acid level, with only four conservative substitutions within their N-termini (Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vandekerckhove and Weber, 1978.

claim: The coding sequences for β- and γ-cytoplasmic actins are different by approximately 13% due to synonymous substitutions.
source: Despite this near-identity, the coding sequences for these two actin isoforms are different by approximately 13% due to synonymous substitutions (Erba et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Erba et al., 1986.

claim: The coding sequence difference between β- and γ-actin can lead to differential arginylation of these two actins.
source: Our work has previously shown that this coding sequence difference can lead to differential arginylation of these two actins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Zhang et al., 2010).

claim: Arginylated β-actin accumulates in vivo.
source: Arginylated β-actin accumulates in vivo, while arginylated γ-actin is degraded (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: Arginylated γ-actin is degraded in vivo.
source: Arginylated β-actin accumulates in vivo, while arginylated γ-actin is degraded (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: β-actin knockout leads to defects in embryogenesis and early embryonic lethality in mice.
source: β-actin knockout leads to defects in embryogenesis and early embryonic lethality (Bunnell et al., 2011; Shawlot et al., 1998; Shmerling et al., 2005; Strathdee et al., 2008; Tondeleir et al., 2013; Tondeleir et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing embryonic lethality in β-actin knockout mice.

claim: γ-cytoplasmic actin knockout mice survive until birth and have much milder overall phenotypic defects compared to β-actin knockout mice.
source: while γ-cytoplasmic actin knockout mice survive until birth and have much milder overall phenotypic defects (Belyantseva et al., 2009; Bunnell and Ervasti, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Belyantseva et al., 2009 and Bunnell and Ervasti, 2010.

claim: β-actin's nucleotide sequence, rather than its amino acid sequence, underlies its essential role in embryogenesis.
source: Our prior work has shown that β-actin's nucleotide sequence, rather than its amino acid sequence, underlies its essential role in embryogenesis (Vedula et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vedula et al., 2017.

claim: Actbc-g/c-g mice (β-coded γ-actin) developed normally and showed no gross phenotypic defects.
source: Such Actbc-g/c-g mice developed normally and showed no gross phenotypic defects, thus demonstrating that the intact β-actin gene, rather than protein, defines its essential role in embryogenesis (Patrinostro et al., 2018; Vedula et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patrinostro et al., 2018 and Vedula et al., 2017.

claim: The intact β-actin gene, rather than protein, defines its essential role in embryogenesis.
source: Such Actbc-g/c-g mice developed normally and showed no gross phenotypic defects, thus demonstrating that the intact β-actin gene, rather than protein, defines its essential role in embryogenesis (Patrinostro et al., 2018; Vedula et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patrinostro et al., 2018 and Vedula et al., 2017.

claim: Cells expressing β-actin migrated at rates similar to wild-type untransfected cells in wound-healing assays.
source: While cells expressing β-actin migrated at rates similar to wild-type untransfected cells in wound-healing assays, cells expressing γ-actin migrated nearly twofold faster.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cells expressing γ-actin migrated nearly twofold faster than cells expressing β-actin in wound-healing assays.
source: While cells expressing β-actin migrated at rates similar to wild-type untransfected cells in wound-healing assays, cells expressing γ-actin migrated nearly twofold faster.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of γ- or γ-coded β-actin led to changes in cell morphology and distribution of focal adhesions.
source: Expression of γ- or γ-coded β-actin led to changes in cell morphology and distribution of focal adhesions, which were larger in size and localized mostly at the cell periphery rather than under the entire cell
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Focal adhesions in γ-actin- or γ-coded-β-actin-expressing cells were larger in size and localized mostly at the cell periphery rather than under the entire cell.
source: Expression of γ- or γ-coded β-actin led to changes in cell morphology and distribution of focal adhesions, which were larger in size and localized mostly at the cell periphery rather than under the entire cell, similarly to previously reported cellular phenotypes linked to poorer cell attachment and faster migration (Kim and Wirtz, 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and supported by citation to Kim and Wirtz, 2013.

claim: Focal adhesions in γ-actin- or γ-coded-β-actin-expressing cells appeared to be poorly anchored and often not visibly associated with long actin bundles.
source: Focal adhesions in γ-actin- or γ-coded-β-actin-expressing cells appeared to be poorly anchored, though often not visibly associated with long actin bundles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: Long actin cables could be clearly seen anchoring focal adhesions in β-actin- or β-coded γ-actin-expressing cells.
source: In contrast, long actin cables could be clearly seen anchoring focal adhesions in β-actin- or β-coded γ-actin-expressing cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: β-actin translation elongation is approximately twofold faster than γ-actin at focal adhesion sites.
source: Single-molecule measurements of actin translation using the SunTag system at the focal adhesion sites showed an approximately twofold faster translation elongation of β-actin compared to γ-actin.
evidence: This is directly measured using SINAPS experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: γ-actin accumulation in cells was slower than β-actin.
source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) demonstrated that γ-actin accumulation in cells was slower than β-actin, further confirming global differences in actin isoform translation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Differences in translation rates can directly impact actin bundle formation, leading to shorter actin bundles in the case of slower translating γ-actin.
source: Molecular simulations of actin assembly at the focal adhesions showed that differences in translation rates can directly impact actin bundle formation, leading to shorter actin bundles in the case of slower translating γ-actin, in agreement with our experimental data.
evidence: This is demonstrated by computational modeling shown in Figure 5 and supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Nucleotide coding sequence-dependent translation rates, coupled to zipcode-targeted actin mRNA localization, play an essential role in differentiating actin isoforms' function in cell migration.
source: Our results demonstrate that nucleotide coding sequence-dependent translation rates, coupled to zipcode-targeted actin mRNA localization, play an essential role in differentiating actin isoforms' function in cell migration.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data showing that both coding sequence and mRNA localization are required for the observed phenotypes.

claim: Cells expressing eGFP-β-actin migrated at rates similar to wild-type untransfected cells.
source: Strikingly, while cells expressing eGFP-β-actin migrated at rates similar to wild-type untransfected cells, cells expressing eGFP-γ-actin migrated nearly twofold faster (Figure 1, top right and bottom; Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cells expressing eGFP-γ-actin migrated nearly twofold faster than cells expressing eGFP-β-actin.
source: Strikingly, while cells expressing eGFP-β-actin migrated at rates similar to wild-type untransfected cells, cells expressing eGFP-γ-actin migrated nearly twofold faster (Figure 1, top right and bottom; Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The difference in cell migration rates between β-actin and γ-actin expressing cells was coding sequence dependent.
source: This difference in cell migration rates was coding sequence dependent, as seen in cells expressing the codon-switched actin variants, γ-coded β-actin (which migrated faster, similarly to those expressing γ-actin), and β-coded γ-actin (which migrated slower, like β-actin-expressing cells) (Figure 1, top left; Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data using codon-switched variants shown in Figure 1.

claim: The effect of actin isoform expression on directional cell migration is mediated by their nucleotide coding sequence and does not appear to be influenced by their amino acid sequence.
source: Thus, the effect of actin isoform expression on directional cell migration is mediated by their nucleotide coding sequence and does not appear to be influenced by their amino acid sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the codon-switched experiments showing that coding sequence determines the phenotype.

claim: The β-actin 3′UTR contains a zipcode sequence that is required for its mRNA localization to the cell periphery.
source: In normal cells, the β-actin 3′UTR contains a zipcode sequence that is required for its mRNA localization to the cell periphery (Kislauskis et al., 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kislauskis et al., 1993.

claim: The β-actin 3′UTR zipcode sequence has been shown to be important for directional cell migration.
source: the β-actin 3′UTR contains a zipcode sequence that is required for its mRNA localization to the cell periphery (Kislauskis et al., 1993) and has been shown to be important for directional cell migration (Condeelis and Singer, 2005; Katz et al., 2012; Kislauskis et al., 1994; Kislauskis et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: γ-actin mRNA has no zipcode sequence and does not undergo targeting to the cell periphery.
source: γ-actin mRNA has no such sequence and does not undergo targeting to the cell periphery (Hill and Gunning, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hill and Gunning, 1993.

claim: Cells expressing actin constructs without the β-actin 3′UTR did not exhibit significant differences in cell migration rates.
source: These cells did not exhibit significant differences in cell migration rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Differences in the effects of cytoplasmic actin coding sequences on cell migration require mRNA targeting to the cell periphery.
source: Thus, differences in the effects of cytoplasmic actin coding sequences on cell migration require mRNA targeting to the cell periphery.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments comparing constructs with and without the β-actin 3′UTR.

claim: In migrating cells, eGFP-β-actin patches appeared more prominent and persisted considerably longer than eGFP-γ-actin patches at focal adhesion sites.
source: Imaging the long-term (hours) behavior of actin at focal adhesion patches during wound healing using TIRF-M revealed that in migrating cells, eGFP-β-actin patches appeared more prominent and persisted considerably longer than eGFP-γ-actin patches (Figure 2A–C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Focal adhesions in eGFP-β-actin-expressing cells persist for longer periods of time than in eGFP-γ-actin-expressing cells.
source: Imaging the long-term (hours) behavior of actin at focal adhesion patches during wound healing using TIRF-M revealed that in migrating cells, eGFP-β-actin patches appeared more prominent and persisted considerably longer than eGFP-γ-actin patches (Figure 2A–C), suggesting that focal adhesions in eGFP-β-actin-expressing cells persist for longer periods of time.
evidence: This is inferred from TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Short-term actin dynamics at the focal adhesions showed no notable differences in focal adhesion recovery rates that correlated with either coding or amino acid sequence.
source: At the same time, testing short-term (5 min) actin dynamics at the focal adhesions using Fluorescence Recovery After Photobleaching (FRAP) showed no notable differences in focal adhesion recovery rates that correlated with either coding or amino acid sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Different actin isoforms affect long-term focal adhesion persistence without strongly affecting short-term focal adhesion or protrusion dynamics during persistent directional migration at the cell leading edge.
source: Thus, different actin isoforms affect long-term focal adhesion persistence without strongly affecting short-term focal adhesion or protrusion dynamics during persistent directional migration at the cell leading edge.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing long-term TIRF data with short-term FRAP data.

claim: In eGFP-β-actin-expressing cells, focal adhesions had a normal elongated morphology and were distributed throughout the entire cell footprint.
source: In eGFP-β-actin-expressing cells, focal adhesions had a normal elongated morphology and were distributed throughout the entire cell footprint.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: eGFP-γ-actin-expressing cells formed focal adhesions that localized mostly at the cell periphery.
source: In contrast, eGFP-γ-actin-expressing cells formed focal adhesions that localized mostly at the cell periphery (Figure 3, top row of images; Figure 3—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Focal adhesions in eGFP-β-coded-γ-actin-expressing cells resembled those in eGFP-β-actin.
source: This trend depended on the actin coding sequence: focal adhesions in eGFP-β-coded-γ-actin-expressing cells resembled those in eGFP-β-actin, while focal adhesions in eGFP-γ-coded-β-actin-expressing cells were like those in eGFP-γ-actin-expressing cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Focal adhesions in eGFP-γ-coded-β-actin-expressing cells were like those in eGFP-γ-actin-expressing cells.
source: This trend depended on the actin coding sequence: focal adhesions in eGFP-β-coded-γ-actin-expressing cells resembled those in eGFP-β-actin, while focal adhesions in eGFP-γ-coded-β-actin-expressing cells were like those in eGFP-γ-actin-expressing cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Most focal adhesions in cells expressing eGFP-β-actin and eGFP-β-coded γ-actin were associated with long thick bundles of actin emanating from the focal adhesion point.
source: Imaging eGFP-actin in widefield showed that most focal adhesions in cells expressing eGFP-β-actin and eGFP-β-coded γ-actin were associated with long thick bundles of actin emanating from the focal adhesion point (Figure 3, top, and Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by widefield microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: The dorsal bundles connecting to the focal adhesions were much less prominent in γ-actin- and γ-coded β-actin-expressing cells.
source: In comparison, the dorsal bundles connecting to the focal adhesions were much less prominent in γ-actin- and γ-coded β-actin-expressing cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by widefield microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: Focal adhesion size uniquely predicts cell migration rate.
source: Focal adhesion size uniquely predicts cell migration rate (Kim and Wirtz, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim and Wirtz, 2013.

claim: Larger focal adhesions correlate with faster migration speeds.
source: Focal adhesion size uniquely predicts cell migration rate (Kim and Wirtz, 2013), with the larger focal adhesions correlating with faster migration speeds.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim and Wirtz, 2013.

claim: Faster migrating cells expressing γ-actin and γ-coded β-actin had significantly larger focal adhesions than slower migrating cells expressing β-actin and β-coded γ-actin.
source: We measured the focal adhesion area in all the four cell cultures transfected with different actin isoforms and found that faster migrating cells expressing γ-actin, and γ-coded β-actin indeed, had significantly larger focal adhesions than slower migrating cells expressing β-actin and β-coded γ-actin (Figure 3, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated by focal adhesion measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: β- and γ-actin coding sequences determine the size and distribution of focal adhesions in migrating cells in a manner that correlates with changes in their migration speed.
source: Thus, β- and γ-actin coding sequences determine the size and distribution of focal adhesions in migrating cells in a manner that correlates with changes in their migration speed.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between focal adhesion properties and migration rates.

claim: Focal adhesions in cells transfected with β-actin and β-coded γ-actin recovered slightly faster than cells transfected with γ-actin and γ-coded β-actin.
source: Focal adhesions in cells transfected with β-actin and β-coded γ-actin recovered slightly faster than cells transfected with γ-actin and γ-coded β-actin (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: Cell spreading and polarization are critically determined by their adhesion to the substrate and correlate with their migratory behavior.
source: Cell spreading and polarization are critically determined by their adhesion to the substrate and correlate with their migratory behavior (Kim and Wirtz, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim and Wirtz, 2013.

claim: Cells expressing eGFP-β-actin had a larger footprint than cells expressing eGFP-γ-actin.
source: Using these shape modes to analyze images of cells expressing different actin isoforms' coding sequences, we found that cells expressing eGFP-β-actin had a larger footprint (Figure 3—figure supplement 8A, clustered to the left of the y-axis)
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell shape analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8A.

claim: Cells expressing eGFP-β-actin had more variance in their polarization than cells expressing eGFP-γ-actin.
source: we found that cells expressing eGFP-β-actin had a larger footprint (Figure 3—figure supplement 8A, clustered to the left of the y-axis) and had more variance in their polarization (Figure 3—figure supplement 8A, spread across the y-axis)
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell shape analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8A.

claim: The footprint size of cells depends on the actin isoform coding sequence.
source: Expression of the codon-switched actin variants, β-coded γ-actin, and γ-coded β-actin showed that the footprint size depended on the actin isoform coding sequence
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell shape analysis using codon-switched variants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8A.

claim: The polarization variance of cells appeared to be amino acid sequence-dependent.
source: Expression of the codon-switched actin variants, β-coded γ-actin, and γ-coded β-actin showed that the footprint size depended on the actin isoform coding sequence, while the polarization variance appeared to be amino acid sequence-dependent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell shape analysis using codon-switched variants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8A.

claim: Cells expressing the γ-actin coding sequence were slightly smaller than those expressing β-actin coding sequence.
source: Cells expressing the γ-actin coding sequence were slightly smaller than those expressing β-actin coding sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 8B, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by measurements of trypsinized cell area shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8B.

claim: The ~6% difference in cell size was far less prominent than the difference in spread cell area, which accounted for a greater than 80% change in the size of cell footprint.
source: This ~6% difference in cell size was far less prominent than the difference in spread cell area (Figure 3—figure supplement 8B, right), which accounted for a greater than 80% change in the size of cell footprint.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing pre-spreading and post-spreading cell areas shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8B.

claim: Cells expressing γ-actin are less spread on the substrate, and this difference in spreading is coding sequence-dependent.
source: Thus, cells expressing γ-actin are less spread on the substrate, and this difference in spreading is coding sequence-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from cell area measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8B.

claim: Computational predictions suggest that the coding region of β-actin mRNA forms a more relaxed secondary structure than that of γ-actin.
source: In search of an underlying mechanism that could link actin isoforms' coding sequence to their intracellular properties, we turned to our previous study that used computational predictions of the mRNA secondary structures for β-actin and γ-actin. This study suggested that the coding region of β-actin mRNA forms a more relaxed secondary structure than that of γ-actin, predicting potential differences in translation elongation rates (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: The recovery rate of eGFP fluorescence after whole-cell photobleaching was significantly faster for eGFP-β-actin compared to eGFP-γ-actin.
source: The recovery rate was significantly faster for eGFP-β-actin compared to eGFP-γ-actin (Figure 4A, top right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Newly synthesized β-actin accumulates in cells faster than γ-actin.
source: Thus, newly synthesized β-actin accumulates in cells faster than γ-actin.
evidence: This is inferred from FRAP experiments showing faster recovery of β-actin.

claim: γ-actin coding sequence showed a nearly twofold higher level of NAPs/mRNA than that of β-actin.
source: γ-actin coding sequence showed a nearly twofold higher level of NAPs/mRNA than that of β-actin (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by SINAPS experiments shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The elongating ribosomes had a twofold higher load, and thus slower translocation rate, over γ-actin mRNA compared to β-actin.
source: γ-actin coding sequence showed a nearly twofold higher level of NAPs/mRNA than that of β-actin (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), indicating that the elongating ribosomes had a twofold higher load, and thus slower translocation rate, over γ-actin mRNA compared to β-actin.
evidence: This is inferred from NAPs/mRNA measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: This is the first characterization of different ribosome loads on individual mRNAs of two protein isoforms that have the same coding sequence length.
source: This is the first characterization of different ribosome loads on individual mRNAs of two protein isoforms that have the same coding sequence length.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The fluorescence recovery rate of individual translation sites was approximately twofold slower for γ-actin compared to β-actin.
source: This recovery rate was approximately twofold slower for γ-actin compared to β-actin (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP of translation sites shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The translation elongation rate of β-actin and γ-actin differs by approximately twofold—faster for β-actin compared to γ-actin.
source: Using both sets of data, we conclude that the translation elongation rate of the two actin isoforms differs by approximately twofold—faster for β-actin compared to γ-actin (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is concluded from both NAPs/mRNA and FRAP measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: A twofold decrease in subunit supply rate resulted in over a twofold decrease in actin bundle length in computational simulations.
source: During 10-min simulations, the time window typically sufficient for establishment of robust focal adhesions, varying actin subunit supply rate resulted in pronounced differences in the length of the actin bundle growing from the focal adhesion site (Videos 5 and 6). A twofold decrease in subunit supply rate resulted in over a twofold decrease in actin bundle length (Figure 5A, right and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by computational modeling shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Actin bundles associated with the focal adhesion sites were markedly longer in β-actin-expressing cells, compared to those expressing γ-actin.
source: To test this prediction experimentally, we measured the length of eGFP-actin-decorated bundles emanating from paxillin-positive focal adhesion patches in cells stably expressing different eGFP-actin isoforms, using both the migrating cells at the edge of the wound and single cells (Figure 5B–D). In both types of cultures, actin bundles associated with the focal adhesion sites were markedly longer in β-actin-expressing cells, compared to those expressing γ-actin (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: The trends in actin bundle length followed the actin coding sequence, rather than the amino acid sequence.
source: Moreover, these trends followed the actin coding sequence, rather than the amino acid sequence (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by measurements using codon-switched variants shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The slower subunit supply dictated by differences in translation elongation rates of β- and γ-actin coding sequences during the initial events of focal adhesion formation and maturation bears direct consequences to cell adhesion and migration.
source: Thus, the slower subunit supply dictated by differences in translation elongation rates of β- and γ-actin coding sequences during the initial events of focal adhesion formation and maturation bears direct consequences to cell adhesion and migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of computational modeling and experimental measurements.

claim: This study constitutes the first direct comparison of translation rates of two closely related proteins.
source: This study constitutes the first direct comparison of translation rates of two closely related proteins and the first demonstration that these translation rates can mediate their functions in vivo.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: This study constitutes the first demonstration that translation rates can mediate protein functions in vivo.
source: This study constitutes the first direct comparison of translation rates of two closely related proteins and the first demonstration that these translation rates can mediate their functions in vivo.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Faster translating β-actin is required for generating stable focal adhesions.
source: Our data show that faster translating β-actin is required for generating stable focal adhesions, while the slower translating γ-actin leads to faster focal adhesion turnover.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing longer persistence of β-actin at focal adhesions.

claim: Slower translating γ-actin leads to faster focal adhesion turnover.
source: Our data show that faster translating β-actin is required for generating stable focal adhesions, while the slower translating γ-actin leads to faster focal adhesion turnover.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing shorter persistence of γ-actin at focal adhesions.

claim: The effects mediated by slower translating γ-actin on cell migration manifest only when the γ-actin mRNA is targeted to the cell periphery via the β-actin zipcode sequence.
source: Importantly, our data also show that the effects mediated by slower translating γ-actin on cell migration manifest only when the γ-actin mRNA is targeted to the cell periphery via the β-actin zipcode sequence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments comparing constructs with and without the β-actin 3′UTR.

claim: Slower translation at the leading edge makes γ-actin less capable of supporting and sustaining strong focal adhesions.
source: We propose that slower translation at the leading edge makes γ-actin less capable of supporting and sustaining strong focal adhesions.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations.

claim: One plausible role of localized fast actin translation at focal adhesions is to balance the competition between actin monomer pools required for protrusion and adhesion formation.
source: Given that rapid polymerization of actin is required for lamellipodium protrusion and focal adhesion formation, one plausible role of localized fast actin translation at focal adhesions is to balance the competition between actin monomer pools required for protrusion and adhesion formation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations.

claim: In γ-actin-expressing cells, most focal adhesions, while larger in area, do not appear to be visibly anchored by prominent actin bundles.
source: In support, in γ-actin-expressing cells, most focal adhesions, while larger in area, do not appear to be visibly anchored by prominent actin bundles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: Cells expressing β-actin contain long actin cables emanating from most of the focal adhesion sites.
source: In contrast, cells expressing β-actin contain long actin cables emanating from most of the focal adhesion sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopy data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 5.

claim: The faster migration rate in γ-actin-expressing cells is caused by weaker cell-substrate attachment.
source: We propose that the faster migration rate is thus caused by weaker cell-substrate attachment in cells expressing γ-actin (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The increase in cell speed in γ-actin-expressing cells is only evident in a wound-healing assay, where cells are collectively stimulated to migrate directionally.

claim: Actin behavior in response to strong signals for cells to polarize and move directionally during wound healing depends on local actin translation more critically than during random migration.
source: It is likely that actin behavior in response to the strong signals for cells to polarize and move directionally during wound healing depends on local actin translation more critically than during random migration, where cells can change directions or remain stationary for extended periods of time and are not constrained in the direction of their polarization and motility.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed differences between wound-healing and single-cell migration.
